components.heading: Linux Lab 03: A deterministic userspace mini-stack

payload.title: A deterministic userspace mini-stack
payload.summary: Send TCP payload chunks through IPv4 and Ethernet framing, route them, inject bounded faults, reassemble bytes, and inspect the final frame over a local Unix datagram socket pair.

prerequisites: Earlier routing, TCP, IPv4, Ethernet, and diagnostics lessons
A Linux environment with AF_UNIX SOCK_DGRAM support
Caller-owned payload, output, route, and fault spans that do not overlap result storage
Finite route, retransmission timeout, attempt, and fault-script inputs
outcomes: Separate deterministic virtual time from wall-clock time and scheduler behavior
Model delivery, drop, delay, reorder, retransmission, duplicate acceptance, and retry exhaustion
Inspect final-frame diagnostics without making diagnostics govern transfer success

payload.exercise: Implement tcpip_linux_l03_run in exercise.c after the starter's scalar and span validation. Preserve predictable result initialization and avoid payload output writes on validation failures.
payload.reference: The solution reuses the course reference targets for routing, IPv4 parsing, TCP construction and checksum validation, state transitions and reassembly, and complete-frame diagnostics.
checks: Clean delivery, first-attempt drop with retransmission, out-of-order chunks, and delayed duplicates succeed deterministically
Retry exhaustion, longest-prefix route selection, insufficient output capacity, and repeated runs are covered
Final diagnostics are mandatory but best effort for formatting capacity
Sanitizer and warnings-as-errors configurations are strongly recommended

allowed: A userspace teaching model using a local AF_UNIX socket pair as a simulated wire
Complete synthetic Ethernet frames inside the local process
Independently authored course code using documented userspace interfaces
excluded: Internet or packet sockets, root access, interface changes, traffic outside the local process, or kernel mutation
MTUs, NIC queues, congestion, real packet loss, full RFC conformance, fragmentation, IPv6, NAT, TLS, persistence, or concurrent endpoints
Interpreting virtual_elapsed_ms as a latency benchmark or pasting Linux kernel code into the lab
